paragraphs: Shapley explanations assign importance to input features by considering how they contribute alongside different combinations of other features. For deep neural networks, calculating these values exactly requires examining all possible feature coalitions. The number of combinations grows exponentially, making this explanation approach expensive as inputs become larger.

The paper introduces SHEAR, which computes explanations using only a small selection of coalitions. Its selection strategy follows a proposed Shapley chain rule and aims to minimize absolute error relative to exact Shapley values. The central idea is to choose informative combinations carefully, so reducing computation also preserves the accuracy of the resulting feature scores.

The evaluation examines three distinct concerns: numerical agreement with exact values, faithfulness of the explanations, and execution speed. SHEAR consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods across the reported metrics. These findings support its potential for explaining neural predictions when computing resources are limited, while grounding that potential in the evaluated settings.
icml-2022-accelerating-shapley-explanati.tldr: SHEAR accelerates Shapley explanations by selecting a small set of informative feature coalitions while preserving explanation accuracy.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients jointly train a model while keeping their local datasets to themselves. This arrangement still requires repeated communication with a server, which can become expensive. The paper also identifies limited adaptivity in updates based on stochastic gradient descent as a separate obstacle to effective training.

Existing approaches address these concerns through different mechanisms: compression or quantization reduces communication, while federated adaptive optimizers change how model updates are made. The authors propose FedCAMS to address both concerns within one method. Its contribution is a communication-efficient adaptive training approach accompanied by a theoretical convergence analysis.

For nonconvex stochastic optimization, the analysis establishes a convergence rate of O(1/√(TKm)), matching the rate of non-compressed counterparts. This means that, in the analyzed setting, introducing communication savings does not worsen the stated convergence order. Experiments across multiple benchmarks support the theoretical analysis, providing empirical evidence alongside the mathematical result for combining compression with adaptive federated learning.
icml-2022-communication-efficient-adapti.tldr: FedCAMS combines communication efficiency with adaptive federated optimization while matching its non-compressed counterparts’ theoretical convergence rate.

paragraphs: An agent observing an environment encounters information that matters for its task alongside distracting variation. This paper asks which information a learned world model should retain. It organizes environmental information along two dimensions: whether the agent can control it and whether it relates to reward, producing four categories.

Within this framework, useful information is defined as both controllable and relevant to reward. The authors use this distinction to clarify what different earlier representation-learning approaches remove. They then introduce Denoised MDPs, a way to learn world models that explicitly separate out certain distracting components, giving the agent a cleaner representation for reasoning and learning.

Experiments use variants of DeepMind Control Suite and RoboDesk. The denoised model performs better than raw observations and the compared prior approaches on policy optimization tasks and on joint position regression, which is not a control task. These results suggest that deliberately filtering observations can produce representations useful beyond the immediate task of choosing actions.
icml-2022-denoised-mdps-learning-world-m.tldr: Denoised MDPs learn world models that separate controllable, reward-relevant information from distractions, improving performance on the evaluated control and regression tasks.

paragraphs: Tissue overlap can hide lesion characteristics in medical images, making disease prediction harder. The paper studies this problem through benign-versus-malignant classification of mammogram masses. Its goal is to learn features that describe the mass even when surrounding gland tissue obscures the visual evidence needed for classification.

The proposed DAB-Net uses alpha blending to generate composite images containing obscured masses. An encoder-decoder framework then separates their representations into mass-related features and interfering gland features. Each feature group must support reconstruction of its corresponding image component. These reconstruction objectives guide the separation, while only the mass-related features are passed to the disease classifier.

Experiments on the public DDSM dataset and three in-house datasets show that the strategy can achieve state-of-the-art performance, with reported AUC improvements of 3.9%–4.4% on obscured cases. Visualization analysis also suggests better separation of masses from glands. Together, these findings support the proposed use of explicit separation to recover diagnostically relevant characteristics under tissue overlap.
icml-2022-disentangling-disease-related-.tldr: DAB-Net learns to separate mammogram mass features from obscuring gland tissue, improving benign-versus-malignant classification in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Vision models based on multilayer perceptrons can recognize images by mixing information across tokens and channels. The paper identifies a weakness in existing versions: their token-mixing operations remain fixed regardless of the content being processed. This limits how the fusion operation adapts to the particular visual input.

DynaMixer generates mixing matrices dynamically from the contents of all tokens involved in the operation. Consequently, the way information is combined depends on what the tokens contain. The architecture also uses dimensionality reduction and a multi-segment fusion mechanism to reduce time complexity and improve robustness while retaining this content-sensitive mixing.

On ImageNet-1K, the 97-million-parameter model reaches 84.3% top-1 accuracy without extra training data, comparing favorably with state-of-the-art vision MLPs. A smaller, 26-million-parameter version achieves 82.7%, exceeding the compared MLP-like models of similar capacity. These results support dynamic mixing as an effective architectural choice at both of the reported model sizes.
icml-2022-dynamixer-a-vision-mlp-archite.tldr: DynaMixer improves vision MLPs by adapting token mixing to image content, with strong ImageNet-1K results at two model sizes.

paragraphs: Neural compression uses learned data distributions to help entropy codecs encode information efficiently. Although this can improve compression ratios over traditional codecs, running the neural network can take enough time to hinder practical deployment. This paper targets that inference cost while preserving the ability to recover the original data exactly.

The proposed Integer-only Discrete Flows, or IODF, build on invertible transformations between discrete variables. The authors design these transformations around 8-bit quantization and integer-only arithmetic. They also add learnable binary gates that remove redundant filters during inference, reducing the amount of network computation required when the compressor is used.

The implementation runs on GPUs through TensorRT. In the reported comparison, IODF achieves a tenfold inference speedup over the fastest existing neural compressors while retaining high compression rates on ImageNet32 and ImageNet64. The findings show how arithmetic choices and removal of redundant computation can address neural compression latency alongside its compression effectiveness.
icml-2022-fast-lossless-neural-compressi.tldr: IODF uses integer-only invertible transformations and learned filter removal to deliver a reported tenfold inference speedup while retaining high lossless compression rates.

paragraphs: Data poisoning changes training data to influence a model’s behavior. Deep Partition Aggregation addresses this threat by training separate classifiers on disjoint data subsets and combining their predictions. Partitioning restricts how dataset distortions can affect the ensemble, allowing robustness guarantees for individual predictions.

The proposed Finite Aggregation changes how those training subsets are constructed. It first divides the data into smaller disjoint pieces, then combines duplicates of these pieces into larger, overlapping subsets for the base classifiers. This construction reduces the worst-case impact of poisoned examples and strengthens the certified robustness bounds. The authors also connect the method to both deterministic and stochastic aggregation defenses.

On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and GTSRB, the method consistently improves certificates while maintaining DPA’s clean accuracies. The reported increases in certified fractions reach 3.05%, 3.87%, and 4.77%, respectively. These gains concern provable protection at the individual-prediction level, showing that reorganizing the ensemble’s training data can strengthen guarantees without sacrificing the reported clean-data accuracy.
icml-2022-improved-certified-defenses-ag.tldr: Finite Aggregation strengthens certified defenses against data poisoning by constructing overlapping classifier training sets from smaller disjoint data partitions.

paragraphs: Screening systems create shortlists so later stages can concentrate resources on promising candidates. The paper asks what guarantees such a system can provide using a classifier, whether that classifier was trained or manually constructed. It shows that perfect calibration alone does not ensure an optimal shortlist for every possible candidate pool.

The authors introduce CSS, which combines any given classifier with calibration data to construct near-optimal shortlists. Its distribution-free guarantee targets a desired number of qualified candidates in expectation. That qualification matters: the result concerns the expected number selected, rather than a promise that every individual shortlist contains the target number.

A further variant calibrates the classifier separately across specified groups and provides provable diversity guarantees for the resulting selections. Experiments using US Census survey data support the theoretical findings and produce better shortlists than several competitive baselines. The contribution connects classifier scores to guarantees about the screening decision itself, including both qualification targets and group diversity.
icml-2022-improving-screening-processes-.tldr: CSS uses calibration data to build near-optimal shortlists with distribution-free guarantees on the expected number of qualified candidates.

paragraphs: Task-free continual learning handles changing data streams without explicit task boundaries while trying to preserve earlier knowledge. Replaying stored examples is a common strategy, but a model can eventually memorize its buffer. The buffer also gives an uncertain picture of past data because it differs substantially from the full history.

This paper proposes evolving the memory distribution to make its contents progressively harder to memorize. It formulates the process through distributionally robust optimization, training against a worst-case evolved memory distribution. Wasserstein gradient flow supplies a way to derive a family of methods that change the buffer’s data distribution within a continuous space of probability measures.

The framework ties its performance guarantee to that worst-case evolved distribution and reports more robust learned features than existing replay methods. Benchmark experiments demonstrate reduced forgetting. The method also shows greater robustness to adversarial examples than the compared task-free continual-learning approaches, suggesting that challenging the model through memory evolution can help both retention and resistance to perturbations.
icml-2022-improving-task-free-continual-.tldr: Evolving replay memory through distributionally robust optimization reduces forgetting and improves reported adversarial robustness in task-free continual learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies large linear least-squares problems with more observations than unknowns. Solving these problems requires balancing computational cost against prediction accuracy. The authors extend iterative Hessian sketching, an approach that reduces computation by approximating part of the optimization problem, into a broader framework called iterative double sketching.

The new framework approximates both the gradient and the Hessian at each iteration. These quantities respectively describe the direction of change and the curvature used by the optimizer. To understand the consequences of approximating both, the authors derive an exact limiting expression for conditional prediction error under Gaussian sketching. This analysis also guides hyperparameter selection.

Using that theoretical result, they design an efficient algorithm based on a new class of sketching matrices related across successive iterations. A non-asymptotic analysis establishes a state-of-the-art trade-off between accuracy and efficiency for the proposed algorithm. The contribution links an error characterization to a concrete optimization method, making the approximations part of an analyzed computational strategy.
icml-2022-iterative-double-sketching-for.tldr: Iterative double sketching approximates both gradients and Hessians, using error analysis to design an efficient least-squares optimizer.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can require substantial experience and may transfer poorly between tasks. Model-based meta reinforcement learning addresses these problems by learning how environments evolve and drawing on experience from previous tasks. This paper examines that framework with particular attention to identifying task dynamics and efficiently finding a useful policy.

The proposed approach uses posterior sampling and combines two components: a graph structured surrogate model, or GSSM, for task dynamics, and an amortized policy optimization step. The dynamics model provides predictions about the task, while the policy-search component is designed to support fast execution without performing policy gradient updates at test time.

The authors report that GSSM achieves competitive dynamics prediction with lower model complexity. Their policy-search approach also obtains high returns while avoiding those test-time updates. These findings address two distinct costs within the framework: the complexity of modeling an environment and the work needed to produce effective behavior when the learned approach is used.
icml-2022-model-based-meta-reinforcement.tldr: A graph structured dynamics model and amortized policy search support competitive prediction and high returns without test-time policy gradient updates.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations describe visual signals through networks that map coordinates to signal values. They can capture detailed images or scenes, but fitting a separate network for each scene can require extensive training and many measurements. This paper seeks to reduce both costs by learning reusable components from a collection of data.

Its Neural Implicit Dictionary consists of coordinate-based subnetworks trained to cover the desired space of functions. A new scene is represented by combining wavelets sampled from that dictionary and solving for their coding coefficients. To train a large group of subnetworks in parallel, the framework uses a mixture-of-experts design with sparse gating.

Experiments report reconstruction of 2D images and 3D scenes two orders of magnitude faster, using up to 98% less input data. The authors also demonstrate image inpainting and occlusion removal. These results show the practical value of moving substantial representation learning into a reusable dictionary, leaving a smaller coefficient-solving problem for unseen scenes.
icml-2022-neural-implicit-dictionary-lea.tldr: A learned dictionary of implicit neural functions enables faster scene reconstruction with substantially fewer measurements in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised image classification uses unlabeled images alongside labeled examples to reduce dependence on annotation. One challenge is deciding which model-generated labels are trustworthy enough to use during learning. The paper adapts neural processes to this setting through a method called NP-Match, combining relationships between examples with uncertainty estimation.

NP-Match implicitly compares data points when predicting labels. Similar labeled examples therefore influence the prediction for an unlabeled image, improving the quality of its pseudolabel. The method also estimates uncertainty, which can guide selection of unlabeled examples whose pseudolabels are reliable. These two capabilities address both generating useful training targets and choosing which targets to trust.

Compared with uncertainty-based methods using Monte Carlo dropout, NP-Match estimates uncertainty with substantially less computational overhead, potentially saving time during training and testing. Across four public datasets, it either exceeds state-of-the-art results or performs competitively. The findings support neural processes as a useful approach to semi-supervised classification, with benefits spanning predictive quality and uncertainty-estimation cost.
icml-2022-np-match-when-neural-processes.tldr: NP-Match uses neural processes to improve pseudolabels and estimate uncertainty efficiently for semi-supervised image classification.

paragraphs: Federated learning allows edge devices to train a shared model while retaining their own data. However, local training consumes device resources, and communication can be constrained by network bandwidth. ProgFed addresses these costs through progressive training, changing the training framework itself to reduce computation and communication in both directions.

The authors prove that ProgFed has the same asymptotic convergence rate as standard training of full models. Their experiments span several convolutional architectures and U-nets, with tasks ranging from classification to medical image segmentation. Across these evaluations, converged models retain strong performance while saving up to 20% of computation and 63% of communication costs.

Progressive training can also be combined with compression techniques, allowing additional choices in the balance between communication and utility. The reported combinations reduce communication by up to fiftyfold with only a 0.1% loss in utility. These results position ProgFed as a complementary training strategy whose resource savings can extend beyond those obtained from compact messages alone.
icml-2022-progfed-effective-communicatio.tldr: ProgFed uses progressive federated training to reduce computation and communication while maintaining strong performance and the standard asymptotic convergence rate.

paragraphs: Heavy Ball is a momentum method that is widely observed to speed up gradient-based training. Explaining that acceleration mathematically has been harder. Earlier proofs largely covered quadratic or nearly quadratic objectives, because the available analysis techniques relied on the Hessian, which describes local curvature, remaining fixed.

This paper develops techniques that explicitly track how the Hessian changes between consecutive optimization steps. By relating those changes to convergence speed, the analysis can go beyond objectives with fixed curvature. The resulting theory identifies a class of Polyak-Lojasiewicz optimization problems for which Heavy Ball has provable acceleration.

The scope of the result is the identified class of problems, with the title highlighting the condition that nonconvexity is averaged out. The analysis also demonstrates a benefit from adjusting the momentum parameter adaptively. Together, these contributions extend the theoretical explanation of momentum’s effectiveness beyond quadratics and connect that explanation to how momentum is chosen during optimization.
icml-2022-provable-acceleration-of-heavy.tldr: New curvature-change analysis proves Heavy Ball acceleration for a class of nonquadratic Polyak-Lojasiewicz problems and supports adaptive momentum.

paragraphs: Domain generalization aims to transfer from observed training environments to unseen ones. This paper approaches the problem by recovering the subspace containing invariant features. Its theoretical comparison uses a linear data model in which existing Invariant Risk Minimization approaches require at least d_s + 1 environments, where d_s measures the dimension of spurious features.

The first proposed algorithm, ISR-Mean, uses class-conditional means to identify the invariant subspace and achieves provable generalization with d_s + 1 environments under that model. ISR-Cov additionally uses second-order information and reduces the required number to O(1). Both methods avoid the nonconvex optimization issues associated with IRM and have global convergence guarantees.

On synthetic benchmarks, the proposed methods outperform IRM. On three real-world image and text datasets, both also work as post-processing procedures for trained models, improving worst-case accuracy under spurious correlations and group shifts. The results combine model-specific theoretical guarantees with evidence that recovering invariant structure can improve existing representations in practical datasets.
icml-2022-provable-domain-generalization.tldr: Invariant-feature Subspace Recovery uses distribution moments to obtain domain-generalization guarantees and improve reported worst-case accuracy under spurious correlations.

paragraphs: The paper studies agents making repeated decisions while trying to avoid unusually high costs. It measures risk using Conditional Value at Risk, or CVaR. Agents receive only the costs of their selected actions, while cost distributions also depend on other agents’ generally unobserved choices, making the relevant risk values difficult to estimate.

The proposed algorithm estimates CVaR by sampling costs and then uses a one-point, zeroth-order procedure to estimate its gradient. This allows risk-sensitive updates without direct gradient observations. The authors prove that the algorithm achieves sublinear regret with high probability, meaning its cumulative regret grows more slowly than the number of decision rounds.

Two variants reuse information from the preceding iteration. One reuses cost samples to improve CVaR estimation accuracy; the other uses earlier CVaR values as residual feedback to reduce gradient-estimate variance. The paper analyzes their convergence and illustrates performance in an online market modeled as a Cournot game, connecting the risk-sensitive learning framework to interacting economic decisions.
icml-2022-risk-averse-no-regret-learning.tldr: The paper develops risk-averse learning algorithms that estimate CVaR from bandit feedback and achieve high-probability sublinear regret.

paragraphs: Adversarially robust image classifiers often produce sharper feature attributions that concentrate more closely on the relevant object. This paper investigates a geometric explanation for that observation. It focuses on decision boundaries, the surfaces where a classifier’s predicted class changes, and on the directions perpendicular to those surfaces.

The authors show that smoother boundaries make nearby input gradients align more closely with boundary normal vectors. Because robust models have smoother boundaries, gradient-based methods such as Integrated Gradients and DeepLift can capture more accurate information about those nearby boundaries. This connects the appearance of an attribution map to the local geometry of the classifier.

The paper then introduces boundary attributions, which aggregate local boundary-normal information to explain a classification. These produce sharper, more concentrated visual explanations even for non-robust models. The findings suggest that the geometric factors associated with robust interpretability can also guide explanation methods directly, extending their usefulness beyond models specifically trained for adversarial robustness.
icml-2022-robust-models-are-more-interpr.tldr: Smooth decision boundaries help explain robust models’ clearer attributions and motivate sharper boundary-based explanations even for non-robust models.

paragraphs: Contrastive adversarial training has improved the robustness of contrastive learning, but evaluating that robustness presents a separate problem. Existing metrics depend on attack algorithms, image labels, and downstream tasks. The paper argues that these dependencies can affect the consistency and reliability of assessments of the learned representation.

The authors propose Robustness Verification for Contrastive Learning, or RVCL, as a framework for addressing this evaluation problem. They also use extreme value theory to investigate how the robust radius of a contrastive encoder relates to the robust radius of a supervised downstream task. This connects robustness of the representation-producing component to robustness of a task built upon it.

Experiments across several benchmark models and datasets support the theoretical findings. They further show that RVCL can assess robustness at both the model level and the individual-image level. The contribution therefore concerns how robustness is measured and related across stages of a learning pipeline, complementing efforts to improve robustness through training.
icml-2022-robustness-verification-for-co.tldr: RVCL evaluates contrastive-learning robustness and uses extreme value theory to connect encoder robustness with downstream-task robustness.

paragraphs: A Stackelberg prediction game represents strategic interaction between a learner and an attacker. With least-squares loss, the problem initially takes a difficult bilevel form. Earlier reformulations permit polynomial-time global solutions through semidefinite or second-order cone programming, but those approaches are poorly suited to datasets with very large numbers of features.

The paper introduces a nonlinear change of variables that rewrites the game as least squares subject to a spherical constraint. It proves that an ε-optimal solution to this formulation, and hence to the original game, can be obtained in approximately O(N/√ε) floating-point operations, suppressing logarithmic factors. Here, N counts nonzero entries in the data matrix.

For practical solution, the authors apply Krylov subspace and Riemannian trust-region methods. Both avoid matrix factorization, making the reformulation suitable for large problems. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report speedups of orders of magnitude over the state of the art, showing how an equivalent mathematical formulation can substantially change computational feasibility.
icml-2022-solving-stackelberg-prediction.tldr: A spherical least-squares reformulation enables factorization-free algorithms that solve the evaluated Stackelberg prediction games orders of magnitude faster.

paragraphs: Value functions describe the returns associated with policies across states. Understanding the shape of the set of possible value functions can inform optimization and representation. This paper studies that geometry for robust Markov decision processes, where uncertainty about state transitions is explicitly included in the problem.

Because earlier geometric approaches do not transfer easily to the robust setting, the authors first revisit ordinary Markov decision processes. They develop a shared perspective that decomposes value spaces state by state into unions of hypersurfaces. For robust value functions, the relevant surfaces are conic, and each contains the values of policies that agree at one state.

The analysis also shows that the extreme points of the transition uncertainty set are sufficient to determine the robust value space. This gives a structural way to characterize that space without requiring every uncertainty-set point in the characterization. The paper further discusses nonconvexity and agreement across multiple states, extending the geometric account of how policy choices relate to robust values.
icml-2022-the-geometry-of-robust-value-f.tldr: The paper characterizes robust value spaces through conic hypersurfaces and shows that uncertainty-set extreme points suffice to determine their geometry.

paragraphs: Gradual domain adaptation moves from a labeled source to an unlabeled target through intermediate unlabeled domains. These intermediate stages can help bridge distribution changes. However, an earlier guarantee for gradual self-training grew exponentially with the number of stages, making the bound uninformative even when that number was only moderately large.

Under more general and relaxed assumptions, this paper establishes a substantially improved target-error bound. Its terms depend on source error, accumulated distributional change TΔ, and sample-related quantities T/√n and 1/√(nT), with logarithmic factors suppressed. The dependence on T is linear and additive in the growing terms, replacing the earlier exponential multiplier.

The result implies an optimal choice of the number of stages and suggests constructing intermediate domains to minimize total path length TΔ. Thus, both how many domains are used and how they connect matter to the analysis. Experiments on semi-synthetic and real datasets corroborate these implications, supporting the theory as guidance for designing adaptation paths.
icml-2022-understanding-gradual-domain-a.tldr: A tighter analysis of gradual self-training reveals how the number and distributional path of intermediate domains affect generalization.

paragraphs: Vision-language pretraining often depends on carefully aligned image-text pairs, which require annotation or substantial cleaning. This paper explores learning from separate image-only and text-only collections. Its goal is to establish connections between the two modalities while reducing dependence on datasets that already contain well-matched pairs.

The proposed cross-modal CutMix replaces visually grounded words in sentences with image patches having similar meanings. This creates a mixed text-and-image view while preserving sentence semantics and increasing data diversity. The inserted cross-modal noise also encourages the model to learn interactions between textual and visual tokens as it learns to denoise the input.

VLMixer combines this augmentation with contrastive learning, bringing the original text view and its mixed counterpart closer together for instance-level alignment. Experiments across five downstream tasks show that VLMixer can surpass previous state-of-the-art unpaired pretraining methods. The findings support using semantically matched local substitutions to help connect modalities when aligned training pairs are scarce.
icml-2022-vlmixer-unpaired-vision-langua.tldr: VLMixer learns from unpaired images and text by replacing words with semantically similar image patches and aligning the resulting views.

paragraphs: Standard transformers face quadratic computational and memory costs as sequence length grows. Sparse attention reduces the number of token connections, but choosing those connections raises a question: how much graph connectivity is needed to preserve performance? This paper develops an analysis tool for examining that trade-off.

The proposed Normalized Information Payload, or NIP, scores how information transfers through an attention graph. The authors use this theoretical perspective to design Hypercube Transformer, whose token interactions follow a hypercube structure. The resulting sparse model has O(N log N) complexity for sequence length N, providing a more favorable scaling pattern than quadratic attention.

Experiments on tasks with different sequence lengths support the proposed graph-scoring function. Hypercube Transformer produces results comparable to, or better than, a vanilla transformer in the reported evaluations. The contribution pairs a concrete sparse architecture with a way to reason about connectivity, helping explain how reduced attention graphs can retain effective information exchange.
icml-2022-what-dense-graph-do-you-need-f.tldr: A graph information-transfer score guides Hypercube Transformer, which achieves O(N log N) complexity with competitive reported performance.

paragraphs: Large language models can perform tasks they were not explicitly trained to solve, but their architectures and training objectives differ substantially. This paper systematically compares those choices for text-to-text models. It examines causal and non-causal decoder-only architectures alongside encoder-decoder models, using autoregressive and masked language-modeling objectives.

The evaluation also distinguishes models used after self-supervised pretraining from those receiving multitask prompted finetuning. The authors train models exceeding five billion parameters for more than 168 billion tokens. This scale is intended to increase the likelihood that the conclusions remain relevant to larger models, rather than establishing that they necessarily transfer.

The strongest choice depends on the training pathway. Causal decoder-only models with autoregressive pretraining perform best after self-supervised training alone. Models with non-causal input visibility, masked pretraining, and subsequent multitask finetuning perform best among the experiments overall. These findings motivate considering adaptations across architectures and objectives, because the preferred configuration changes with whether multitask finetuning is included.
icml-2022-what-language-model-architectu.tldr: The best tested language-model configuration for zero-shot generalization changes depending on whether multitask prompted finetuning follows pretraining.
